claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate using hierarchical-microstructure descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate can predict the specified properties within 10–20% of experimental values.
The surrogate can operate at least ten times faster than full-scale DFT- or MD-based simulations.
The HfNbTiVAl10 material is produced by vacuum melting and heat treatments that develop a hierarchical heterostructure with distinct phases and internal precipitates.
SEM and TEM measurements can quantify phase-boundary spacing, precipitate size and distribution, interface density, and other hierarchical features for use as model inputs.
The size, spatial distribution, and volume fraction of secondary phases or precipitates govern dislocation pinning in HfNbTiVAl10.
Interface density and phase connectivity govern load transfer and stress concentration in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical features influence the elastic response and Young’s modulus of HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical precipitates and interfaces influence the yield response through control of dislocation mobility.
Nano-precipitate size, interface density, and phase connectivity control crack initiation and fracture behavior in HfNbTiVAl10.
A hierarchical FCC/L12 microstructure can strengthen an alloy through pinning of superdislocations by internal FCC precipitates.
Physics-based models combining linear elasticity and microscopic principles have been shown to predict strengthening and ductility.
Replacing atomistic simulations with a physics-informed ML surrogate minimizes computational cost.

Direct DFT evaluation of alloy fracture or yield strength is mostly beyond currently available implementations, and first-principles calculations for disordered multi-principal-element alloys remain challenging.
Direct DFT/MD simulations are established full-scale predictive baselines for all three proposed outputs, including fracture toughness.
The model may fail when microstructural descriptors are not reproducible across nominally similar samples.
The model may fail when emergent phases or transformations are absent from its training data.
The model may fail when environmental degradation or specimen-scale effects dominate mechanical behavior.
Small processing changes may alter the quantitative relationship between microstructural metrics and macroscopic mechanical responses.
Previous machine-learning models in related alloys provide a basis for anticipating the claimed efficiency gain.
